lead: A communication system carries information from one point to another: a source produces a message, a transmitter conditions it, a channel carries it, and a receiver hands it to a destination. The channel is rarely kind — it attenuates the signal, adds noise, and is shared with other users. Modulation is the deliberate shift of the message spectrum onto a carrier frequency so the signal fits the channel, the antenna and the spectrum rules. Every phone call, UPI confirmation and cricket live stream uses these same blocks.
prereq: You need: a sinusoid, frequency, wavelength and the relation v = fλ from first-year physics.

sections.h3: The block schematic of a communication system

blocks.text: A communication system moves information from a source to a destination. Information is whatever the destination does not already know: a voice, a temperature reading, a UPI transaction record, a frame of video. The system is drawn as blocks in a line, and some syllabi call this drawing the communication model.

The source produces the message. The transducer converts it into an electrical voltage — a microphone turns sound pressure into a voltage, a camera sensor turns light into charge. The result is the message signal m(t), a voltage that varies with time t measured in seconds.

The transmitter prepares the signal for the channel: it amplifies, filters and modulates. The channel is the physical medium — a copper pair, a coaxial cable, an optical fibre, or free space. The receiver amplifies what arrives, removes the carrier and produces an estimate of m(t). The destination is a human ear, a screen or a storage device.

blocks.where: r(t) is the received voltage; s(t) is the transmitted signal after the channel has attenuated it; n(t) is the unwanted noise voltage added by the channel and by the receiver's own circuits.

blocks.text: Noise is random, so it is described by statistics, not by a formula — see 1.6. Digital systems insert two more blocks between source and transmitter: a source encoder that compresses bits and a channel encoder that adds protection; see Unit 4 and Unit 7.

sections.h3: Baseband, passband, and modulation as frequency translation

blocks.text: A signal whose spectrum lies from 0 Hz up to some maximum B hertz is a baseband signal. Speech, music and sensor outputs are baseband: their energy sits near 0 Hz. A passband signal has its spectrum concentrated around a carrier frequency fc far above 0 Hz.
Modulation translates the message spectrum to sit around f<sub>c</sub>. It creates no new information; it only moves the information to a new place in the spectrum.
s(t) = A(t) cos(2π f<sub>c</sub> t + φ(t))
blocks.where: s(t) is the modulated (passband) signal; A(t) is its slowly varying envelope in volts; f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier frequency in hertz; φ(t) is its slowly varying phase in radians; t is time in seconds.

blocks.text: The carrier is the sinusoid cos(2π fc t). It carries no information by itself; it only provides a place in the spectrum. The message rides on it through A(t) or φ(t).

If A(t) varies in proportion to m(t), the scheme is amplitude modulation. If the instantaneous frequency or phase varies with m(t), it is angle modulation, that is, frequency or phase modulation. These are the analog modulations. In digital modulation the same two quantities are switched between a finite set of values (see Unit 6). The bandwidth Bs of the modulated signal is the width of spectrum it occupies; for amplitude modulation Bs ≈ 2B. The bandwidth is set by the message and the scheme, not by fc.

items: Antenna size. An antenna radiates efficiently when its length is a good fraction of the wavelength λ = c/f, where c = 3×108 m/s is the speed of light and f is the radiated frequency in hertz. A quarter-wave antenna is λ/4 long. At audio frequencies this is kilometres; at radio frequencies it is centimetres. The worked example below computes both.

Frequency assignment. Free space is shared by everyone. Regulators license bands (mobile services in India use bands around 900 MHz, 1800 MHz and 2.5 GHz) so that each transmitter stays inside its own slot. Modulation is what puts a signal into its assigned slot.

Multiplexing. Many messages share one channel when each is placed on a different carrier: frequency division multiplexing (see Unit 2). Time division multiplexing shares the time axis instead (see Unit 4).

Noise and interference. Modulation does not remove noise. It moves the signal to a band where interference is low, and it lets the receiver filter out everything outside fc ± Bs. Wideband schemes then trade bandwidth for noise immunity (see Unit 3).

blocks.text: The receiver's band-pass filter passes only the band around f<sub>c</sub>. Signals at other frequencies are rejected before they reach the detector, which is the practical gain of putting the message on a carrier.

figure.caption: The message travels down the chain from source to destination. Noise enters at the channel and adds to whatever arrives at the receiver.

examples.question: A 1 kHz audio tone has to be radiated from an antenna. (a) Find its wavelength and the length of a quarter-wave antenna. (b) The same tone now modulates a 100 MHz carrier. Find the wavelength and quarter-wave antenna length of the radiated wave. Take c = 3×10⁸ m/s.
steps: Use λ = c/f. At f = 1 kHz = 1×10³ Hz: λ = (3×10⁸ m/s) ÷ (1×10³ Hz) = 3×10⁵ m = 300 km.
Quarter-wave length = λ/4 = 300 km ÷ 4 = 75 km. An antenna 75 km long cannot be built on a tower, so direct radiation of the audio tone is impossible.
At the carrier f<sub>c</sub> = 100 MHz = 1×10⁸ Hz: λ = (3×10⁸ m/s) ÷ (1×10⁸ Hz) = 3 m.
Quarter-wave length = λ/4 = 3 m ÷ 4 = 0.75 m, that is 75 cm. This is a small, practical antenna.

The radiated wave is now at 100 MHz; the audio information rides on it as a variation of the envelope A(t). The antenna shrank by a factor 75 km ÷ 0.75 m = 1×10⁵, exactly the ratio of the two frequencies.
examples.answer: At 1 kHz: λ = 300 km and λ/4 = 75 km. At 100 MHz: λ = 3 m and λ/4 = 0.75 m — modulation shortens the antenna by a factor of 10⁵.

traps: Modulation does not create information and does not by itself improve the signal-to-noise ratio at the receiver input. It only shifts the message spectrum and makes the antenna and multiplexing practical.
Do not confuse the carrier frequency with the message frequency. The carrier decides where the signal sits in the spectrum; the message and the scheme decide the bandwidth.
In λ = c/f, put the frequency that is actually radiated. After modulation that is f<sub>c</sub>, not the audio frequency.
Noise enters at the channel and in the receiver's front end. It is not generated mainly by the transmitter, and a strong transmitter does not remove it.
Baseband does not mean audio. Any signal whose spectrum starts at 0 Hz, including a digital NRZ pulse train, is a baseband signal.

quiz.q: List the blocks of a communication system in order from source to destination.
quiz.a: Source, transducer, transmitter, channel, receiver, destination. Noise adds at the channel.

The carrier is the high-frequency sinusoid cos(2π f<sub>c</sub> t) that places the signal in the spectrum. The message signal m(t) is the baseband voltage produced by the source and transducer; it carries the information.

quiz.q: Why must a baseband audio signal be modulated before free-space transmission?
quiz.a: Its wavelength at audio frequency is hundreds of kilometres, so a quarter-wave antenna is tens of kilometres long. Modulation moves the spectrum to a radio frequency where λ/4 is under a metre, and it lets the receiver filter out other users.

quiz.q: Modulation does not improve the signal-to-noise ratio at the receiver input. State three things it does achieve.
quiz.a: It makes the antenna physically realisable, it places the signal in an assigned frequency slot so many users can share the medium by frequency division multiplexing, and it allows the receiver to band-pass filter out interference outside its own band.

quiz.q: A 4 kHz message is transmitted by amplitude modulation on a 10 MHz carrier. Find the carrier wavelength, the quarter-wave antenna length and the approximate bandwidth of the modulated signal.
Two stations in one city each carry a 5 kHz audio message by amplitude modulation. Explain why they cannot both use a 1 MHz carrier.
quiz.a: Each modulated signal occupies about 2B = 10 kHz around its carrier, that is 0.995 MHz to 1.005 MHz. Two signals on the same carrier occupy the same band, so their spectra overlap and neither receiver can separate them. The carriers must be spaced by at least the sum of the half-bandwidths, and the regulator assigns different carriers.

quiz.q: A system sends a 5 kHz message over a cable at baseband; another sends the same message on a 1 GHz carrier over free space. Which needs more bandwidth and which needs a larger antenna? Justify.
quiz.a: Both need roughly the same bandwidth, since bandwidth is set by the message and the scheme, not by the carrier. The baseband cable system needs only an electrode or a small coupler, but a free-space system needs an antenna of order λ/4 = 7.5 cm at 1 GHz. Without the carrier, an antenna for 5 kHz would be about 15 km.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems split these blocks into software: a software defined radio samples the passband signal and does the mixing, filtering and demodulation in code, so the same hardware serves many standards. In 5G and Wi-Fi the carrier is in the gigahertz range, which is why handsets hold several small antennas and why millimetre-wave links need line of sight. Spectrum is auctioned as a national resource, and the price of a band is really the price of the carrier. Search for software defined radio, spectrum auction, and link budget to go further.
